Yesterday
YES-ter-day
n. and adv.
From Saxon gestran daeg, the day before this. Webster 1828: the day last past; the day next before the present. Scripture uses it for the brevity of man’s knowledge, the brevity of a thousand years before God, and the unchangeableness of Christ.

Biblical Definition

Yesterday is one of Scripture’s measuring words, and it is used to measure three different things. It measures how little men know: For we are but of yesterday, and know nothing, because our days upon earth are a shadow (Job 8:9) — spoken by Bildad, and true in itself even though he applied it wrongly. It measures a millennium from God’s side: For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night (Psalm 90:4), in the psalm of Moses, the oldest in the Psalter, which sets God’s eternity against a lifespan of seventy years and asks Him to teach us to number our days. Peter quotes the same measure to answer scoffers about the delay of the second coming. And most importantly it measures Christ, who is not measured by it at all: Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever (Hebrews 13:8). The verse sits between a command to remember dead leaders and a warning against strange doctrines, which is exactly where it is needed: teachers pass, teachings shift, and the Object of faith does not.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines YESTERDAY as the day last past; the day next before the present; and figuratively, a short time past or lately.

expand to see more

YESTERDAY, n. — The day last past; the day next before the present.

As an adverb, on the day last past; as, he came yesterday.

Figuratively, a very short time past; recently; as, we are but of yesterday.

In Scripture, used to express both the brevity of human life and the shortness of long ages before God.

From Saxon gestran, yester, and daeg, day — the root of yesteryear and yestereve.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 13:8 — "Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever."

Psalm 90:4 — "For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night."

Job 8:9 — "(For we are but of yesterday, and know nothing, because our days upon earth are a shadow:)"

Isaiah 35:10 — "And the ransomed of the LORD shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads: they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away."

Modern Corruption

Hebrews 13:8 is quoted constantly to guarantee that whatever God did in a past revival or in an apostle’s ministry He is obliged to repeat, when the verse is about the immutability of Christ’s Person and is set as a guard against novel doctrines.

expand to see more

The context governs the meaning and it is usually skipped. Verse 7 says Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation. Verse 8 says Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, to day, and for ever. Verse 9 says Be not carried about with divers and strange doctrines. The leaders die; the Christ they preached does not change; therefore do not go chasing novelties. The verse is a doctrinal anchor, not a warrant for expecting particular phenomena. Used the popular way it proves far too much: God has not repeated the plagues of Egypt, the crossing of the sea, or the giving of the law, and no one supposes His immutability requires Him to.

Psalm 90:4 corrects a different distortion. Peter applies it directly to those who mock the delay of Christ’s return: one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward (2 Peter 3:8-9). The apparent delay is not indifference and it is not incapacity; it is patience with a purpose, and the purpose is that men should come to repentance. Job 8:9 supplies the posture that follows from both verses. We are of yesterday and know nothing — which was Bildad’s truest sentence, and he ruined it by using it to accuse a righteous man.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ethmol (H865), yesterday; temol (H8543), yesterday, formerly; Greek chthes (G5504), yesterday; echthes, the same.

expand to see more

Hebrew ethmol (H865) — yesterday, in time past; we are but of yesterday (Job 8:9).

Hebrew temol (H8543) — yesterday; often paired with shilshom for the idiom in time past.

Greek chthes (G5504) — yesterday; Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever (Hebrews 13:8).

Greek ho autos — the same; the emphatic phrase of Hebrews 13:8, also used of God in Hebrews 1:12.

Hebrew ashmurah (H821) — a night watch; as a watch in the night (Psalm 90:4).

Usage

"Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever (Hebrews 13:8) — set between dying leaders and strange doctrines."

"A thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday (Psalm 90:4) — the measure Peter applies to the delay of the coming."

"We are but of yesterday, and know nothing (Job 8:9) — Bildad’s truest sentence, wrongly applied."
